title: CTEs: Name Every Step
objective: After this lesson you will be able to rewrite any nested derived-table query as a flat, named WITH pipeline — chaining multiple CTEs where each step feeds the next — and explain when a CTE beats a subquery, a view, or a repeated expression.
why: Chapter 1's derived tables work, but three levels of parentheses are write-only code: nobody can review them, debug them, or reuse a middle step. Analysts and backend engineers structure the same logic as a pipeline of named steps instead. WITH is the single most readability-improving keyword in intermediate SQL — it turns nesting into a story told top to bottom.

blocks.text: A **common table expression (CTE)** is a named temporary result defined up front with **`WITH`**, then used like a table in the main query. It computes exactly the same thing as Chapter 1's derived table — but the logic reads **top to bottom** instead of inside out. Compare the two shapes solving the same problem (courses with 3+ enrollments):

blocks.code:
-- BEFORE: derived table (Chapter 1) — read inside-out
SELECT per_course.title, per_course.n
FROM (
  SELECT c.title AS title, COUNT(e.id) AS n
  FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id
  GROUP BY c.id
) AS per_course
WHERE per_course.n >= 3
ORDER BY per_course.n DESC;
blocks.caption: The nested version: the real logic hides in the middle

blocks.code:
-- AFTER: CTE — the same query, told as two named steps
WITH per_course AS (
  SELECT c.title AS title, COUNT(e.id) AS n
  FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id
  GROUP BY c.id
)
SELECT title, n
FROM per_course
WHERE n >= 3
ORDER BY n DESC;
blocks.caption: The CTE version: name the step, then use the name

blocks.text: Three mechanical rules. **One:** `WITH name AS ( query )` comes before the main `SELECT` — the CTE is defined first, used second. **Two:** the CTE's column names are whatever the inner SELECT produces (`title`, `n`), and the outer query addresses them directly. **Three:** the outer query can treat `per_course` exactly like a table — filter it, join it, sort it.

blocks.caption: How the database reads a WITH query
nodes: WITH block: define named steps top to bottom
Main query: use the names like tables
Executor: inline each CTE where referenced

blocks.text: One CTE is a rename. **Multiple CTEs are a pipeline**: each step builds on the previous one, and the final SELECT reads like a summary of the analysis. Comma-separate them after a single `WITH` — and note that later CTEs may reference earlier ones, but never the reverse.

blocks.code:
-- Question: which roles produce the most completed learning,
-- and how does each role compare to the overall average?
WITH completions AS (
  -- Step 1: completed enrollments per developer
  SELECT e.developer_id AS dev_id, COUNT(*) AS done
  FROM enrollments e
  WHERE e.completed = 1
  GROUP BY e.developer_id
),
role_stats AS (
  -- Step 2: average completions per role (builds on Step 1)
  SELECT d.role AS role, AVG(completions.done) AS avg_done
  FROM developers d JOIN completions ON completions.dev_id = d.id
  GROUP BY d.role
),
overall AS (
  -- Step 3: one number — the global average (builds on Step 1)
  SELECT AVG(done) AS avg_all FROM completions
)
-- Step 4: the answer — each role vs the global bar
SELECT r.role, ROUND(r.avg_done, 1) AS avg_done,
       ROUND(o.avg_all, 1) AS global_avg
FROM role_stats r CROSS JOIN overall o
ORDER BY r.avg_done DESC;
blocks.caption: Three CTEs feeding one final SELECT — try untangling this with nested parentheses

blocks.text: Read it as a story: *completions* counts per developer, *role_stats* averages by role, *overall* computes the global bar, and the final SELECT compares. Each step is independently runnable — highlight any single CTE body, run it alone, inspect its rows. That debuggability is the entire point: when a pipeline's answer looks wrong, you binary-search the steps instead of staring at parentheses.

blocks.title: The sandbox debugging habit
blocks.text: When a multi-CTE query misbehaves, run each CTE body standalone in the sandbox from top to bottom until the rows stop looking right — every step is a flat SELECT, so the sandbox runs each one. The first step whose output surprises you is where the bug lives. Professionals debug pipelines forward, never by re-reading the whole query.
CTE vs subquery vs view: choosing the tool

All three package a query for reuse — they differ in **scope and lifetime**. A subquery lives inside one statement and is invisible elsewhere. A **CTE** lives for exactly one statement too, but its steps are named, ordered, and individually testable — reach for it the moment nesting passes one level. A **view** (`CREATE VIEW …`) persists in the database for every future query: use it when many queries need the same logic (Lesson 7 builds them properly), not for one-off analysis.

rows: Single value or membership test inside a bigger query
Two or more steps, or anything a teammate must review

blocks.text: Column aliases and the ORDER BY trap

Two details that bite everyone once. **First**, you can rename a CTE's columns at the definition site — `WITH w(total, n) AS (…)` — which is handy when the inner SELECT produces awkward expression names. The alias list must match the column count exactly, or the database errors immediately.

blocks.code:
-- Renaming at the definition site (2 columns out, 2 names given)
WITH per_course(title, n) AS (
  SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.id)
  FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id
  GROUP BY c.id
)
SELECT title, n FROM per_course WHERE n >= 3;
blocks.caption: CTE column aliases: the name list must match the SELECT list one-to-one

blocks.text: **Second**, `ORDER BY` belongs at the very end — on the outer query, not inside the CTE. An ORDER BY inside a CTE body is at best ignored and in some engines an outright error, because a CTE is a *set* of rows and sets have no order until somebody asks for one. Sort where you present, never where you compute.

blocks.title: A CTE is not a performance trick
blocks.text: In SQLite and PostgreSQL a CTE is conceptually inlined where referenced — it does not cache results or speed anything up. If you reference the same CTE three times, expect roughly three evaluations (PostgreSQL 12+ may materialize automatically when it helps, but never rely on it). Choose CTEs for readability and debuggability; reach for indexes and query restructuring — SQL Advanced territory — for speed.

CTEs have one superpower nothing else in this chapter has: a CTE can reference *itself*. That **recursive CTE** (`WITH RECURSIVE`) walks trees and graphs — org charts, category hierarchies, dependency chains — in pure SQL. The syntax needs care (a base case plus a step case, and a termination guarantee), so it gets its own lesson in SQL Advanced. For now, just file the name: when someone says 'we need the whole subtree', the answer starts with `WITH RECURSIVE`.

blocks.query: SELECT c.title AS title, COUNT(e.id) AS n FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id;
blocks.note: Run this CTE body standalone in the sandbox — every CTE step is a flat SELECT, so steps run here. The full WITH assembly targets a real database (PostgreSQL or SQLite): name this step per_course, then SELECT the rows with n >= 3.

items: WITH names each step up front; the main query reads top to bottom instead of inside out
Chain CTEs with commas — later steps can use earlier ones, and every step runs standalone for debugging
Use CTEs over nesting once logic passes one level; use views (Lesson 7) when logic must persist across queries
Column aliases at the definition site must match the SELECT count exactly
ORDER BY goes on the outer query — sets have no order until presentation
CTEs optimize for humans, not machines: no caching is promised

exercise.prompt: The team lead asks: 'Show me developers who completed MORE enrollments than the average developer — name, completed count, and how far above average they are, most-above-first.' Build it as a two-CTE pipeline: (1) completions per developer, (2) the global average over step 1 — then a final SELECT computing the difference. Verify each CTE body standalone in the sandbox, assemble the full pipeline in PostgreSQL or SQLite, and sanity-check: every shown difference must be positive.
hints: Step 1 is identical to this lesson's completions CTE: COUNT(*) WHERE completed = 1, GROUP BY developer_id. Get that running standalone first.

Step 2 averages step 1's counts: SELECT AVG(done) AS avg_all FROM <step1>. The final SELECT joins each developer's row against that single average — CROSS JOIN works because step 2 has exactly one row.
The difference column is done - avg_all, filtered with WHERE done > avg_all and sorted with ORDER BY <difference> DESC. Join developers for names.
exercise.solution:
WITH completions AS (
  SELECT e.developer_id AS dev_id, COUNT(*) AS done
  FROM enrollments e
  WHERE e.completed = 1
  GROUP BY e.developer_id
),
overall AS (
  SELECT AVG(done) AS avg_all FROM completions
)
SELECT d.name, c.done, ROUND(c.done - o.avg_all, 1) AS above_avg
FROM completions c
JOIN developers d ON d.id = c.dev_id
CROSS JOIN overall o
WHERE c.done > o.avg_all
ORDER BY above_avg DESC;
exercise.why: The pipeline mirrors the question's grammar: 'per developer' becomes the GROUP BY step, 'the average' becomes the scalar-over-step-1 CTE, and 'more than' becomes the outer WHERE. CROSS JOIN against a one-row CTE is the idiomatic way to make a global constant available to every row — and the positivity sanity check (WHERE done > avg_all) doubles as the correctness proof: an empty or negative difference would mean the filter or the average is wrong.
exercise.code:
-- Two-CTE pipeline: per-developer counts, then vs-average
WITH completions AS (
  SELECT e.developer_id AS dev_id, COUNT(*) AS done
  FROM enrollments e
  WHERE e.completed = 1
  GROUP BY e.developer_id
),
overall AS (
  SELECT AVG(done) AS avg_all FROM completions
)
SELECT d.name, c.done, ROUND(c.done - o.avg_all, 1) AS above_avg
FROM completions c
JOIN developers d ON d.id = c.dev_id
CROSS JOIN overall o
WHERE c.done > o.avg_all
ORDER BY above_avg DESC;

quiz.q: What is the fundamental readability difference between a derived table and an equivalent CTE?
options: CTEs run faster because the database caches them
The CTE names each step up front so logic reads top to bottom; the derived table nests inside-out
CTEs can return multiple tables at once
There is no difference at all
quiz.explain: Same result, same statement lifetime — the win is entirely human. Named steps can be read, reviewed, and run standalone; triple-nested parentheses cannot. (And no, CTEs promise no caching — that warn callout exists for a reason.)

quiz.q: In WITH a AS (…), b AS (SELECT … FROM a …) SELECT … FROM b, which references are legal?
options: b can use a, but a cannot use b — later CTEs see earlier ones only
a and b can freely reference each other
Only the final SELECT may reference any CTE
quiz.explain: CTEs form a pipeline, not a web: each step sees the steps defined above it. Forward references fail. (The one exception — a CTE referencing itself — is recursion, which needs WITH RECURSIVE and gets its own lesson in SQL Advanced.)

quiz.q: Where does ORDER BY belong in a WITH query, and why?
options: Inside each CTE, so every step stays sorted
Only on the outermost query — CTEs produce unordered sets until presentation
ORDER BY is forbidden with WITH entirely
quiz.explain: A CTE body denotes a set of rows, and sets have no order. Sorting inside is at best discarded work and in some engines an error. Sort once, at the end, where rows meet the reader.

quiz.q: WITH w(total, n) AS (SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT role) FROM developers) — when is this valid?
options: Always — alias lists are just documentation
Only when the alias count matches the SELECT column count exactly (here 2 and 2, so valid)
Only in PostgreSQL, never in SQLite
quiz.explain: Definition-site aliases are a real rename mechanism in both SQLite and PostgreSQL, but the contract is strict: one name per output column. A mismatch is an immediate error, which is actually a feature — it catches SELECT-list edits that would otherwise silently shift meanings.

summary: WITH turns nested queries into named pipelines: define each step once, chain steps with commas, debug each step standalone, and sort only at the end. CTEs live for one statement (views persist — Lesson 7), promise readability rather than speed, and their one superpower — self-reference — unlocks recursion in SQL Advanced.
next: Pipelines shape rows — but sometimes you need to stack result sets on top of each other instead. Next: set operations (UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT), duplicate semantics, and when stacking beats joining.
